section_summary: The section concludes an economic analysis arguing that Japan depended heavily on American scrap iron and lacked practical alternative sources of scrap, pig iron, or iron ore; it includes statistics on supplies from Korea, Manchuria, British Malaya, Australia, the Philippines, China, French Indochina, and New Caledonia. Subsequent correspondence reports Phillips Petroleum Company's July 1940 deliveries of neohexane, iso-octane, and other petroleum products to Mitsui for export to Japan. The final letters transmit and acknowledge an article about a successful 1918 embargo against Japan as a precedent for measures short of war.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on Japan's dependence on imported scrap and iron ore
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan could replace American iron and steel scrap with domestic or foreign iron ore and pig iron.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates that American scrap accounted for roughly one-third of Japanese steel production and argues that other scrap or pig-iron markets could not replace it. Japan would need five to six million tons of additional ore to compensate for two million tons of American scrap, but its domestic and Korean deposits were limited, low-grade, and difficult to expand. British Malaya, Australia, the Philippines, and China offered uncertain supplies because of wartime export controls, possible parallel sanctions, and the Sino-Japanese conflict. A concluding table gives Japanese iron-ore imports by supplying country for 1937–1939, while the report also notes the United States' own need to conserve scrap for national defense.

subfiles.title: Phillips Petroleum Company report of July deliveries for export to Japan
subfiles.from: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green, Chief, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reports petroleum-derived materials delivered to Mitsui & Co. during July 1940 for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: In compliance with a January 8 request, Phillips Petroleum reports deliveries to Mitsui & Co. of 3,300 drums of commercial neohexane, 12,308 drums of commercial iso-octane, and 3,192 drums of products occurring naturally in petroleum. The total was 18,800 drums, each holding 53 gallons.

subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the company's report of July petroleum-product deliveries to Mitsui for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department acknowledges receipt of the August 2 letter. It restates the reported quantities of commercial neohexane, commercial iso-octane, and naturally occurring petroleum products delivered to Mitsui & Co. for export to Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmission of article on the successful 1918 embargo against Japan
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Encloses an Amerasia article presenting the 1918 embargo against Japan as a precedent for contemporary measures short of war.
subfiles.summary: Roger S. Greene sends Ballantine a reprint from the August 1940 issue of Amerasia. The enclosed article by Henry H. Douglas, entitled “A Bit of American History—Successful Embargo Against Japan in 1918,” is recommended as a useful historical precedent at a time when measures short of war were under discussion.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Roger S. Greene's article enclosure
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Acting Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks Greene for sending the Amerasia reprint concerning the 1918 embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine acknowledges Greene's August 14 letter and its enclosed August 1940 Amerasia reprint. He states that Henry H. Douglas's article on the successful 1918 embargo against Japan was read with interest and expresses appreciation for Greene's courtesy.
